data.title: Sky Protocol Faces $2B USDS Withdrawal Wave As $518M Illicit Fund Claims Emerge
data.description:
Sky Protocol processed more than $2 billion in USDS stablecoin redemptions on Thursday, coinciding with a CoinDesk investigation linking $518 million in transactions through its infrastructure to wallets associated with hackers, sanctioned entities and other illicit actors.

Circulating supply of Sky's USDS stablecoin dropped to about $3.16 billion from $5.24 billion in a day, per DefiLlama, the same day as a Nov. 19 report on illicit-linked flows through Sky. Sky said its Peg Stability Module "has processed over $968 billion in volume since inception" and that the alleged figures would be roughly 0.03% of that. https://t.co/0nqbzXFAqP

— Laura Shin (@laurashin) November 20, 2026

The withdrawals saw users exchange Sky's USDS stablecoin for Circle's USDC through its Peg Stability Module (PSM), which allows holders to swap the tokens at a fixed rate. Despite the scale of the redemptions, Sky maintained that USDS held its $1 peg throughout the withdrawals, while pushing back against the investigation's findings.

The development places Sky under increased scrutiny as the protocol faces questions over its exposure to illicit crypto transactions and the resilience of its stablecoin infrastructure.

Sky Processes $2 Billion in USDS Redemptions as Scrutiny Intensifies

Sky said on Friday that the amount of USDC held in its PSM never fell below $800 million during the withdrawals and had climbed back above $1.1 billion. The protocol also maintained that its PSM continued to facilitate USDS-to-USDC exchanges at a 1:1 rate throughout the redemption wave.

We’re aware of the recent CoinDesk report on activity involving the Sky Protocol Peg Stability Module (PSM), predominantly via third-party permissionless platforms. Reports like this are taken seriously across the Sky Ecosystem. For scale: the PSM has processed over $968 billion in volume since inception. The alleged figures would represent roughly 0.03% of that. The PSM is open, onchain infrastructure that supports the USDS and DAI peg by swapping stablecoins 1:1. Within Sky Ecosystem, associated Sky Agent front ends such as @sparkfinance, @grovedotfinance, @SkyMoney and @OseroHQ block users in sanctioned jurisdictions by screening and blocking flagged wallets. Participants across the Sky Ecosystem will continue doing their part alongside the rest of DeFi.

— Sky (@SkyEcosystem) November 19, 2026

However, the withdrawals coincided with concerns raised by CoinDesk's investigation that Circle could freeze USDC held by Sky, potentially making it more difficult for users to redeem their stablecoins.

The investigation, published on Nov. 19, examined research by blockchain analytics firm Inca Digital, which identified $518 million in transactions involving wallets linked to hackers, sanctioned entities and other threat actors over five years. Around $101.9 million of the flagged activity was reportedly associated with North Korean actors, including wallets connected to the February 2025 Bybit hack.

EXCLUSIVE: North Korean hackers and other illicit actors routed $$518M through Sky’s Peg Stability Module, converting freezable $$USDC into unfreezable $$DAI and $$USDS, with $101.9M directly linked to wallets including those behind the Bybit hack, per Inca Digital. @sndr_krisztian reports.

— CoinDesk (@CoinDesk) November 19, 2026

The report also raised questions about the potential exposure of Sky's infrastructure to illicit activity, putting additional scrutiny on the protocol as billions of dollars in USDS redemptions were processed.

Sky Pushes Back Against $518M Illicit Transaction Findings

Sky challenged the investigation's findings, pointing to an assessment by Block Analitica, a risk adviser to the Sky ecosystem, which disputed several aspects of the report.

Block Analitica argued that the $518 million in flagged transactions represented less than 0.06% of the more than $960 billion processed through Sky's Peg Stability Modules. The firm also noted that approximately two-thirds of the identified activity occurred between 2021 and mid-2024, before Sky introduced its newer LitePSM system.

Binance: more than $6 billion in crypto gone on 29 october - and it started with a job interview. in the clip below, co-CEO Richard Teng walks CNBC through the attack. first answer: "well first of all it shouldn't have happened." june: the hackers set up a fake developer tool, and one Binance engineer installed it. september: "they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer." the coding exercise hid malware. per Teng, the FBI has attributed it to North Korea. asked if one laptop was the single point of failure: "no, that's not true. so this is not one single mistake" Binance says it has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets from its own reserves. about $3 billion was reportedly frozen. this week the hackers' wallets moved about $594 million in ether to fresh addresses. $6.34 billion out, 98% put back by the exchange itself - safer to hold money there now, or less?

— Elliot (@htfworld1) November 22, 2026

The risk adviser further questioned the reported connections to North Korean threat actors, arguing that some wallets were several transactions removed from known addresses and could have belonged to unrelated users.

It also pointed out that many of the flagged transactions passed through third-party trading services, including 1inch, ParaSwap and MetaMask Swaps, which automatically select where transactions are routed.

Your favorite crypto project is about to get hacked by a North Korean trained to hack since age 7 This is how North Korea’s human hacker factory works: Stage 1: > Regime scouts brightest math students (7yo) > Top 50 students go to Kumsong High School > 70% of Kumsong's curriculum: computers > Students wear military uniforms from day one Stage 2: > The absolute best go to Mirim College > 5 years at North Korea's secret hacker school > Train in Java, Windows exploitation > Many still don’t know they’re being trained as state hackers Stage 3: > Sent to China to learn the free internet > Study Western communication culture > Get perks that keep you loyal > Master LinkedIn and X norms, DeFi, crypto Congrats, you return as a state cyber soldier

— fabiano.sol (@FabianoSolana) October 30, 2026

These findings form part of Sky's response to the allegations, although Block Analitica's assessment does not independently establish that all flagged transactions were unrelated to illicit activity.

Sky Defends $9.3B in Stablecoin Backing Assets Despite Withdrawals

The redemption wave coincided with a sharp contraction in USDS circulation, with its supply falling nearly 40% in a single day to approximately 3.2 billion tokens, according to DefiLlama data. Despite the decline, USDS continued to trade at its $1 peg.

Sky's stUSDS pays 44.74% on USDS today. Its 4 biggest holders can withdraw exactly $0. The rate rose 5 days in a row: 14.45% on Nov 17, 24.74% on Nov 19, 44.74% now. What I read onchain: • stUSDS deposits: $161.6M • Lent to borrowers against staked SKY: $161.56M, 99.98% of deposits • maxWithdraw() returns 0 for the 4 largest holders (13.07M stUSDS between them) • New deposits are still open: $56.4M of room under the $218M cap So the 44.74% is not a farm. It is the price of an exit that stays shut until SKY borrowers repay or new USDS comes in. The plain savings version from @SkyEcosystem, sUSDS, still pays 3.80% on $2.05B, and you can leave whenever you want. On Saturday I had stUSDS at 34.74% with deposits flat (quoted). Still flat. Would you lock USDS at 44.74% with no exit date, or keep 3.80% with one?

— DeFi Mago (@defi_mago) November 22, 2026

CoinDesk also reported that a wallet linked to crypto exchange Poloniex accounted for a substantial share of the withdrawals, although it remained unclear whether the exchange itself was behind the transactions.

Meanwhile, Sky's combined circulating supply of USDS and DAI fell to $6.11 billion as of Nov. 20, marking a 37.8% decline over the preceding 30 days.

$920M worth of SKY is currently staked through Sky Protocol. Stakers are accessing up to 6.7% in rewards while keeping their position usable for governance delegation and USDS borrowing. One position. More utility for the SKY you already hold. https://t.co/HVVkVLOqcV

— Sky.money (@SkyMoney) November 17, 2026

Despite the contraction, Sky said it held approximately $9.3 billion in assets backing its stablecoins as of Friday, compared with the $6.11 billion in circulating USDS and DAI. Its financial dashboard also showed approximately $93 million in reserves intended to help cover potential losses.

The figures form part of Sky's effort to demonstrate that its stablecoin ecosystem remains adequately backed despite the significant redemptions and scrutiny over its exposure to potentially illicit transactions.

data.title: Is nobody buying cryptocurrencies anymore? Where will Binance find its next growth engine?
data.description:
Author: danny；Source: X，@agintender

April 2021, midway through the bull market. Coinbase was about to ring the Nasdaq bell, Bitcoin reached $60,000, and crypto users had plenty of stablecoins in their pockets, asking every day: Where's the next new story?

Introduction: Did you know? Binance sold the same Tesla stock twice

Binance conveniently added Tesla to its trading interface. The product was called "Stock Token," issued by the German licensed institution CM-Equity, priced in BUSD, and supported fractional shares.

For crypto enthusiasts who had never opened a US stock account, a few clicks were all it took to gain exposure to Tesla's price. Coinbase, Apple, and Microsoft subsequently listed it. However, it fizzled out after just three months – multiple regulators issued warnings, and finally, on July 16th, Binance discontinued the service. Five years later, Tesla is back. In June 2026, Binance launched bStocks, issued by its affiliated company BTech Holdings Limited, with custodian shares backed one-to-one and structured as tokenized securities. Within compliance limits, it can be transferred to the BNB Smart Chain wallet; starting in October, more bStocks were directly added to the Cross Margin and Portfolio Margin collateral lists. This reveals Binance's recurring strategy over the past decade: First, demand grows wildly externally, then Binance lowers the barrier to entry, leveraging its existing user base, funds, and liquidity to expand the market and achieve comprehensive coverage. Then, competitors follow suit, forming an even larger liquidity network. If we examine Binance's product development path since 2017, we'll find that Binance has repeated this strategy countless times. How effective has it been? It's a bit like Xiahou Dun defending a city – turning a blind eye a few times, sometimes brilliant moves, sometimes just paying tuition. First, six things done over nine years. If we look at Binance's nine-year product history, it essentially boils down to six things: finding new profit opportunities, turning those opportunities into low-barrier-to-entry products, keeping funds in pools, channeling BNB holders' interests into demand, selling trading capabilities to institutions, and ensuring the entry point remains in their hands when the next wave of opportunity arrives. Following the years, these six things are crystal clear – like Xiahou Dun reading the Spring and Autumn Annals. Of course, this is hindsight, or a retrospective analysis of business logic. Many products were simply reactive responses to competition, market conditions, and regulatory pressure. Binance's strength lies in its ability to always bring back existing users, funds, and trading networks, regardless of the reasons for new market innovations. Sometimes this is due to its own strength, and sometimes it's due to competitors' mistakes. In any case, this model of attracting users through the "wealth effect" at the front end and converting traffic into sustainable business through trading, retention, and institutional services at the back end has become the starting point for this money-printing machine.

II. 2017-2018: ICOs handle token issuance, Binance handles the trading.

In 2017, issuing a token was easier than setting up a farmers' market. Ethereum smart contracts drastically reduced the cost of token issuance, and ICOs at that time raised billions of dollars.

That was in 2017, when Bitcoin's peak was less than $15,000. The ensuing problem was that there were too many cryptocurrencies on the market, but a lack of reasonably liquid trading venues; retail investors were envious of the price charts but didn't know where to buy or sell. Binance itself was a product of this wave. In July 2017, it raised approximately $15 million through an ICO for BNB and launched its platform that same month. Unfortunately, on September 4th, China halted ICOs and cleaned up domestic platforms. Binance hastily moved its team and servers overseas, inadvertently becoming one of the earliest globally-oriented trading platforms. It capitalized on a simple need: allowing users in mainland China to buy and sell new assets without regulation. Crypto-to-crypto trading, rocket-like listing speeds, efficient matching, multilingual interfaces, and rebates—every step resonated with Asian users. Later, as market depth increased, it attracted another wave of projects and retail investors. In late 2017, Bitcoin reached $20,000, and Binance's new users were so numerous that its servers were practically smoking, even briefly suspending new user registration in January 2018—can you imagine business being so booming that users needed to be turned away? BNB's function at that time was to reduce transaction costs: a 0.1% fee, and a 50% discount for payments made with BNB. But from the perspective of token holders, BNB, from day one, was betting not only on discounts, but also on the exchange's ability to print money. That same year, Launchpad tested two token sales, BREAD and GIFTO. Then, the 2018 bear market arrived, Bitcoin plummeted to around $3,200, and ICOs largely went to zero. Binance faced for the first time the existential question that would haunt it for the next eight years: New tokens weren't appreciating, there was no wealth effect? ​​Why would users come back? III. 2019: A Fire in a Bear Market, Spreading Like Wildfire On January 28, 2019, BTT went on sale on Launchpad. The approximately $7.2 million allocation was split into two sessions, BNB and TRX, which sold out in 13 minutes and 25 seconds and 14 minutes and 41 seconds respectively, causing the system to lag at times. After the ICO boom, the market lacked a wealth effect, and BTT proved that exchanges could create this miracle. At the same time, BitMEX was the leading derivatives platform, with its perpetual contract trading volume dwarfing its spot trading volume, making everyone envious. Binance made two strategic moves that year. First, BNB was transformed from a "coupon for saving transaction fees" into a "ticket to participate in new token offerings." Two months later, Launchpad changed to a lottery system: the number of lots was linked to historical BNB holdings, and successful bidders paid in BNB. Project teams wanted users, and retail investors wanted listing opportunities and liquidity; both sides hit it off, and BNB became the ticket to quick riches. The reason for holding BNB changed from "saving a little money" to "not missing out on getting rich." According to statistics, Launchpad completed 11 sales throughout the year, with the platform having over 15 million users and 184 tokens and 591 trading pairs listed in the spot market. Second, in September, BTCUSDT perpetual contracts were launched, subsequently expanding to USDT-margined and coin-margined structures. Around the same asset, trading relationships multiply: market makers manage cross-market inventory, arbitrageurs borrow coins, adjust margins, connect to APIs, etc., further expanding trading volume and asset accumulation. With more assets accumulated, how to retain them? Thus, Margin, Lending, and Staking were launched in the same year, and Loans were launched in 2020. In Lending's first batch of 14-day products, BNB, USDT, and ETC offered annualized returns of 15%, 10%, and 7% respectively. Combined with P2P, fiat currency entry points, and the BUSD issued in September in partnership with Paxos, a complete internal funding chain is established: Fiat currency enters to buy coins → borrowing money or opening contracts to amplify exposure → idle assets are put into wealth management to earn interest → one-click exchange for stablecoins; from then on, people and funds no longer need to leave the platform. Binance thus began to break free from its dependence on the idea that "only a bull market in spot trading guarantees success." Two other key moments occurred that year: the theft of approximately 7,000 Bitcoins in May, fully covered by the SAFU fund; and the launch of Binance Chain and Binance DEX in April. In retrospect, this was a microcosm of exchanges' early attempts at DeFi, and also a precursor to Binance's aspirations for decentralized infrastructure. Every wave of hype fades, but the accounts, balances, and trading habits left behind can become the starting point for the next business. IV. 2020-2021: Opportunities Beyond Exchanges In June 2020, Compound issued COMP, igniting the DeFi Summer. Total value locked (TVL) surged from less than $1 billion at the beginning of the year to tens of billions of dollars by the end, and Ethereum gas became exorbitantly expensive, costing tens or even hundreds of dollars per transaction – akin to buying groceries by rocket. This posed a threat to Binance beyond just a few fewer transactions: token issuance, trading, lending, and mining all operate in a closed loop on-chain, turning exchanges from an essential step into an optional one. Binance quickly adjusted its strategy, employing two tactics.

  • One Chain: In September 2020, PancakeSwap launched BSC, which is compatible with EVM and has extremely low transaction fees. PancakeSwap then absorbed small and medium-sized funds that were blocked by Ethereum's high gas fees. BNB was also upgraded to smart contract fuel and staking asset.

  • One Chain for In-Site Yield Encapsulation: In the same month, Launchpool was launched, and two months later, BNB Vault was launched. The cumbersome process of installing wallets on the chain, cross-chain operations, and calculating impermanent loss was simplified to a single click of "staking" within the platform, preventing funds from leaving the site.

The 2021 bull market pushed this structure to its peak. BNB soared from less than $40 to nearly $700.

The 2021 bull market pushed this structure to its peak. BNB soared from less than $40 to nearly $700.

In the same year, BEP-95 introduced real-time burning, and at the end of the year, Auto-Burn was launched, etc. The bull market also brought a wave of "anything goes" expansion: the NFT market, fan tokens, blockchain games, Pay, Card, stock tokens, etc., were launched in rapid succession. Basically, whatever was trending in the market, they chased. The result was naturally severe divergence: fan tokens ended abruptly, Pay remained lukewarm, NFT services shut down in 2026, and stock tokens disappeared after three months. The summer of 2021 finally brought regulatory scrutiny from multiple countries, meaning that Xiahou Dun had targeted and locked onto the issue—the speed advantage of 2017 turned into a risky exposure in 2021.

V. 2022-2023: Users not only ask about returns, but also how those returns are transferred

2022 saw a series of collapses: Terra crashed in May, wiping out approximately $40 billion in market value; Celsius and Three Arrows Capital defaulted and went bankrupt in June and July; and FTX collapsed in a week in November. Industry concerns shifted from "where the returns are high" to "where the money is, who can access it, and who will compensate us if something goes wrong."

VII. A Hidden Theme: Selling Trading Capabilities to Others

The bustling retail market is merely a facade, because everyone knows that large funds and institutions are the main players: Since 2019, Binance has continuously provided trading, account, financing, and payment capabilities to institutions. This hidden theme doesn't require stories of 100x coins, but it answers the question, "If retail investors can't find the next wealth story, what will sustain the exchange's business?"

The starting point was the large-scale OTC transactions in January 2019, reportedly involving at least 20 BTC per transaction.

The starting point was the large-scale OTC transactions in January 2019, reportedly involving at least 20 BTC per transaction.

Then came four steps: Becoming an infrastructure provider: In September 2019, Broker was launched, later known as Binance Link; in February 2020, Binance Cloud was launched; and in 2022, MT4/MT5 bridging was established. The logic was B2B wholesale; rather than acquiring customers one by one, it was better to serve enterprises with a massive user base. In September 2026, Exchange Link was incorporated into Crypto-as-a-Service, transforming from "connecting to Binance" to "embedding encryption modules into other people's products." **Moving Institutional Organizational Structure into Accounts:** Managed Sub-Account, already documented in December 2021, separates investor and trader permissions. Binance Fund Manager, launched in July 2022, aggregates trading volume and BNB holdings across related funds to boost VIP status. Binance Wealth, launched in October 2024, serves high-net-worth clients. Fund/Portfolio Accounts, launched in April 2025, aggregates funds by strategy and calculates unit net asset value. **Providing Algorithmic Execution and Financing:** TWAP/POV algorithmic trading was launched in 2023. Spot trading supports FIX API and Drop Copy in August 2024. Financing options include VIP Loans and Institutional Loans, allowing up to 10 sub-accounts to be included in the same risk credit line. **Trading and Custody Completely Separated:** Following FTX, institutions are strictly controlling exchange concentration. In 2023, MirrorX mirrored Ceffu custodial assets onto trading accounts, and Banking Triparty placed collateral in third-party banks. In June 2025, MirrorRSV strengthened independent cold wallets and on-chain verifiable holdings. According to Binance's data, its registered institutional users grew by nearly 97% in 2024. Furthermore, Binance Pay connects with merchants, and Binance Pool (launched in 2020 and now shut down) facilitates miner output and financing, allowing Binance to reach real-world businesses whose primary business is not cryptocurrency trading.

VIII. 2025-2026: Crypto Native Assets Are No Longer Selling, So Take Over Assets from Outside the Crypto World

In July 2025, the US signed the GENIUS Act, and BlackRock and Franklin Templeton turned their money market funds into on-chain tokens; the profitability of altcoins in the crypto world declined. The question became: Can we bring in traditional high-quality assets?

Learning from the lessons of 2021, Binance will first resolve regulatory issues before launching products. In January 2026, under the Abu Dhabi ADGM structure, three licensed entities will share the functions of exchange, clearing and custody, and brokerage. Subsequently, it will launch TradFi perpetual contracts for gold, silver, and stocks, and in June, it will launch bStocks, expanding the margin collateral scope of bStocks in October.

The asset portfolio has since evolved into five layers: crypto spot, crypto perpetual, TradeFi perpetual, bStocks (a tokenized security that integrates spot trading with BSC and collateral), and DAT (the BNB reserve company) stemming from external capital markets. The institutional side has seen quieter yet more significant changes: In February 2026, Franklin Templeton announced that qualified clients could use tokenized money market fund shares on the Benji platform as off-exchange collateral to participate in Binance trading through Ceffu. Franklin Templeton RWA has upgraded from a "trading instrument" to a "funding base for trading." AI is the latest entry point in 2026. Binance launched AI Agent Skills, and in September, Pay Onchain launched enterprise deposits and Agent Pay based on x402. This is both chasing trends and paying off the "menu debt" incurred from a decade of expansion—dozens of products piled up in the app, making it like Xiahou Dun looking at Louis XVI—endless and overwhelming for the average person. The Agent has turned "finding the menu" into "receiving a task." However, at present, expecting a straight line between "AI Agent call growth" and "BNB price surge" is like a eunuch discussing state affairs—utter nonsense. It depends on the actual demand. On October 29th, this system underwent an extreme stress test: Binance experienced a major security incident. A preliminary report on November 3rd stated that approximately $6.34 billion in assets were affected, of which approximately $2.85 billion was frozen or intercepted, with Binance bearing the financial losses itself. Compared to the theft of 7,000 BTC in 2019, the impact was two orders of magnitude larger, but Binance withstood it.

Nine, Two Funding Lines Across Ten Years: BNB Manages Equity, Stablecoins Manage Turnover

Looking at the product development path over the past nine years, two main lines have run through it all.

BNB is responsible for continuously providing users with reasons not to sell: from a 50% discount on transaction fees in 2017, to the Launchpad lottery in 2019, Launchpool and BSC fuel in 2020, Auto-Burn in 2021, Fund Manager institutional VIP in 2022, to the Megadrop/HODLer airdrop in 2024 and the BNB Reserve Company in 2025.

The underlying logic: Binance's business expansion – increased BNB use cases – holders receiving rewards. Stablecoins facilitate the movement of money between products. USDT has been present from the beginning, while Binance's focus on supporting stablecoins has shifted five times: 2017: Relying on USDT → 2019: Launching BUSD and forcibly converting to USDC in 2022 → 2023: BUSD minting stopped, FDUSD took over → December 2024: Partnering with Circle to promote USDC → And now, the latest supporter, United Stables, or U. Just after switching from USDC to BUSD, Binance reconciled with Circle and then launched a new brand, U. This move illustrates one thing: Binance truly prioritizes settlement and liquidity. What matters is which logo is displayed on the front page – the core operations remain while the personnel change. Circle's prospectus sets a price for this relationship: a one-time fee of $60.25 million to Binance, plus monthly incentives linked to USDC balances and benchmark interest rates. The payers have expanded from project teams in 2019 to fund issuers in 2024. To elaborate further, the launch of BFUSD in 2024, along with WBETH, BNSOL, and USDe, further eliminates the choice between "earning interest" and "using as collateral." However, while maximizing capital utilization, collateral valuation discounts and liquidation liquidity become significant risks. This will be evident to everyone on October 11, 2025.

10. The wool comes from the pig: Who pays for the money users earn?

Behind the question of whether the wealth effect can continue is a simple math problem: Who is paying for the extra money in users' accounts?

Does the project team subsidize users for free? How could that be? Business is all about the exchange of interests.

VCs invest to pay team salaries and marketing fees, while users receive tokens. When the tokens are cashed out, the ones paying are the buyers in the secondary market. Why do these buyers buy in? Because they believe the pool is large enough that there will be another buyer. Ultimately, with each new round of rewards, someone has to foot the bill in the secondary market.

XI. Looking Back: The Same Strategy Used Six Times

Reviewing nine years, Binance rarely takes the initiative to be the first to try something new. Its secret weapon is to lower the barriers to entry after external demand is validated, drive down the price, and then amplify it using existing resources:

But what's being poured in are potential customers, not ready-made market depth—how to market traditional stock contracts and how to quote prices during market closures all have to be rebuilt every time.

However, not every attempt is successful. Binance Chain and DEX, which were developed in 2019, gradually became marginalized. The burden of maintaining both chains was heavy, and after migrating functionality to BSC, Beacon Chain officially ceased operations on December 3, 2024. The NFT market, blockchain games, and decentralized storage have followed similar paths. The difference between catching the wave and not catching it lies in whether a temporary impulse can be transformed into sustained demand: perpetual demand, centered around standardized assets, has created a whole set of mutually reinforcing financial needs; NFTs, with their non-standardized nature and extremely thin depth, failed to survive the hype. Therefore, a complete business loop is: Attract new users with opportunities → Increase transaction frequency with transactions → Retain users with financial tools → Bind rights with BNB → Open capabilities to a larger market. Understanding this loop reveals where the next round of growth will lie. The real growth point is never in the "next hot trend," but rather in the most acute internal contradictions at the current stage. Binance's most acute contradiction right now is that it holds excessive distribution capacity, while the supply of crypto-native assets is no longer enough to feed this machine. The fatal flaw is that its original audience and holders are still hoping this approach can continue indefinitely. As a result, everyone is forced to take fragmented steps, developing new businesses while simultaneously protecting BNB's interests—resulting in failing at both ends. Relying on issuing more airdrops to existing users is merely transferring funds within the existing pool; growth is destined to return to zero once subsidies end. Therefore, Binance's next breakthrough lies in using its well-developed trading structure to absorb massive external assets, focusing on three areas: traditional asset trading, OTC collateral, and stablecoin balances. Looking deeper, the real value behind these three points isn't the act of "listing," but rather the pricing power of the collateral. Traditional assets, stablecoins, and tokenized funds can theoretically be listed on any exchange, but "what discount each of these assets is worth in a $34 trillion margin trading system" is determined only by the largest exchange. Whether pricing off-exchange assets like Franklin Templeton or future pricing of illiquid small-cap stocks, the amount of leveraged purchasing power they can generate is not determined by the issuer, but by Binance's margin risk control table. Once this pricing power works, it will reshape the upstream supply inversely by improving capital efficiency. The transmission process is quite direct: when Binance's risk control table approves a higher margin discount rate for a certain type of asset, the cost-effectiveness of holding it for large funds instantly becomes maximized—allowing them to both earn underlying interest and leverage trading. Funds will naturally vote with their feet, flowing to assets that are "more usable and more valuable" within the Binance system. Upstream issuers will soon realize that the success of a product depends not only on the asset itself, but also on whether it meets Binance's collateral requirements and achieves the highest possible discount rate. Listing determines what users can buy, while margin rules determine what users can do with their assets. Thus, Binance's role has undergone a qualitative change: Previously, it was about speed, transferring assets issued by others to the exchange; later, it began to directly influence which assets were more worthwhile to issue and hold through margin pricing. Others issue assets, Binance prices those assets, and then prices assets outside the crypto sphere—this is how it truly transformed from "taking on the challenge" to "setting the challenge." bStocks and TradeFi have perpetually introduced US stocks and commodities, connecting margin collateral and on-chain circulation. The question now is how many people will continue trading after the incentives expire. Regarding off-exchange collateral, tokenized funds, Ceffu, and bank-backed collateral keep traditional large-scale trading relationships within Binance, allowing assets to generate market depth without needing to be listed on exchanges. As for stablecoin balances, from USDC distribution revenue sharing to the newly supported U, the essence is to transform massive amounts of idle funds into a long-term interest-bearing pool. As for Agents, currently only the operational interface has been changed; new uses for funds are yet to be revealed. Most airdrop activities remain simply providing an extra round of rewards to existing users; let's wait and see. Binance's problem over the past decade has been: how to get more people involved in new markets? The question for the next decade is: when opportunities are no longer scarce, why will users still need you?

data.title: After the market experienced a 2.5 billion yuan liquidation, is this the bottom?
data.description:
Author: Blockchain Knight; Source: X, @BlocKnight21

Bitcoin experienced another sharp sell-off over the weekend, falling to around $55,500 at one point, a two-year low, before quickly rebounding and climbing back above $60,000. This drop also triggered over $2.5 billion in leveraged liquidations.

After the sharp drop and rapid rebound, the market naturally began discussing again whether this was the bottom.

But instead of rushing to guess the lowest point, it's better to look at the logic behind identifying the bottom and find direction from it.

Contrarian investment master Templeton proposed the maximum pessimism theory.

He believes that the best opportunities in the market often arise when pessimism reaches its extreme. When investors no longer believe the market can rebound and even begin to sell at any cost, asset prices may be significantly undervalued. In the current market, the Fear & Greed Index has fallen into the extreme fear zone, and investors' concerns about Fed policy, tech stock valuations, and capital outflows from the crypto market are deepening. However, pessimistic sentiment does not mean the market has bottomed out immediately. More importantly, it's crucial to observe whether investors' reactions begin to weaken as bad news continues to emerge, and whether prices are no longer easily broken by negative news. Howard Marks' cycle theory offers another perspective. In his view, market sentiment always oscillates between extreme optimism and pessimism, and extreme sentiment often pushes prices away from reasonable levels. The current pressure on Bitcoin is not only from within the crypto industry. The proposed correction in US tech stocks and market concerns about further tightening by the Fed are also suppressing risk assets. The question is, how much of these negative factors have not yet been priced into the market? Another master, Graham's margin of safety theory, is also worth considering in the crypto market. Market price does not equal asset value; investors need to pay attention to the distance between price and value. Bitcoin lacks corporate profits and cash flow, making it impossible to directly apply traditional valuation methods. However, some on-chain data can still help us determine the market's valuation position. These are not Bitcoin's intrinsic value, but they can reflect the extent to which the market has experienced valuation suppression. If the above theories focus on sentiment and valuation, then Wyckoff's theory focuses more on the selling pressure itself. According to his accumulation model, after a sustained decline, the market may experience panic selling, with a large number of sell orders being released in a concentrated manner, followed by a price rebound. However, a single price spike is not enough to confirm the bottom; the key is to observe the subsequent second test. This is also something worth observing in the current Bitcoin price movement. Whether the rapid rebound over the weekend was a temporary correction after leverage clearing or a sign that selling pressure is waning requires further information from subsequent price action. In addition, ETF fund flows and whether the US stock market can stabilize are also worth monitoring. After all, the crypto market is no longer an isolated market, and macro liquidity will continue to influence Bitcoin's pricing. While the theories of several investment gurus differ, they all point to one question: What exactly changed after the market decline? Has pessimism been fully released? Have negative factors been priced in? Has selling pressure begun to weaken? These are the essential factors behind the price movement, but sometimes the candlestick chart may have already told the whole story.

data.title: Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang: Superintelligence is Coming
data.description:
Author: Alexandr Wang, Chief AI Officer, Meta; Translated by: Jinse Finance Claw

>

Superintelligence is coming. How humanity acts in the coming year will greatly influence the kind of world we will live in.

I have spent a significant portion of my life in mathematics and science. In my view, the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis clearly marks the beginning of a major revolution. For most people who have studied mathematics, this represents the absolute pinnacle of intellectual achievement—in terms of pure intellectual strength and power, nothing humanity has accomplished before can compare to proving the Riemann Hypothesis. I grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, and many physicists would agree: compared to the Riemann Hypothesis, building the atomic bomb is just a homework problem. The significance of this discovery we just witnessed cannot be overstated—and it was achieved with the help of an "alien mind" that we don't understand. For those who have participated in math competitions, there was a similar moment of "Oh no, everything is about to change" when OpenAI o3 in December 2024 enabled models to consistently achieve perfect scores on the AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination). The most difficult problems in the AIME, in terms of intellectual difficulty alone, far exceed the problems that even the top engineers and business professionals face daily. Of course, for models to achieve breakthroughs in other fields, domain-specific knowledge, context, know-how, and other tactical constraints are needed; but the lack of raw intelligence is not a bottleneck. In fact, over the past two years, as we have gradually filled in these "non-intellectual factors," progress in other fields has been tremendous—programming has been almost completely mastered, extremely powerful network capabilities have emerged, and powerful intelligent agents have made models universal and useful assistants. The key insight here is actually quite simple: the most difficult AIME problems are intellectually extremely challenging, far more so than most programming jobs, most cybersecurity jobs, and most business jobs. And for the past two years, we've been bridging these gaps, enabling our models to accomplish these tasks. It's important to note that AIME is merely an extracurricular activity for teenagers; the Riemann Hypothesis, on the other hand, is arguably the most intellectually demanding problem ever posed by humankind, with some of the most brilliant minds dedicating their lives to it over the past 150 years. At MIT, my professors would probably say that the most difficult intellectual problems in almost every major field of human knowledge are "easier" than the Riemann Hypothesis, despite the additional challenges they present, such as experimentation, data, and feedback loops. For models to significantly outperform humans in every field, the remaining gap is no longer intelligence, but rather domain-specific know-how, infrastructure, and experimentation. This means that AI is likely to become the biggest contributor to progress in almost every field, far surpassing even the best humans. It's worth noting that this likely applies equally to AI research itself. Most researchers would agree that AI research demands far less intelligence than proving the Riemann Hypothesis. Models will obviously be smart enough to automate all AI research and clearly surpass humans in self-improvement—while also significantly accelerating research in biology, weapons, economics, and so on. The impact will be enormous. Just as the mathematical community has not yet fully digested the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, almost every field could be accelerated at a rate exceeding human comprehension and oversight. At this moment, it becomes incredibly important to seriously consider what kind of future we want and how to get there. It's hard to imagine humans maintaining control over a completely unrestrained, recursive, self-improving system. It's equally hard to imagine humans maintaining control over a superintelligence that is 1000 times smarter and more capable than humans in every field. We have now reached a juncture: the scientific and technological challenges to capability advancement have likely been solved. Therefore, we must not only make progress in extremely pressing areas such as security, alignment, and safety, but also begin to carefully consider: how should we move forward? I have noticed a particularly pronounced sense of complacency within the AI ​​industry: the belief that ASI is inevitable, and the only problem to solve is how to build it safely. But the stakes go far beyond that. We should not comfortably accept the "handover" of society to AI. We should strive to build a technology that brings a positive future to humanity, empowering everyone with greater autonomy. I firmly believe this is achievable, but it will likely require the entire industry to take actions substantially different from the current "default path."

data.title: Verifying the "scientific drama" of AI Claude and Lean
data.description:
Author: Xiaojing, Tencent Technology

On November 21st, the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement announcing the completion of the formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and expressing full confidence in its correctness.

A day earlier, mathematician Levent Alpöge published the proof completed in collaboration with Claude. This problem, which has plagued the mathematical community for 167 years, has achieved a major breakthrough in a rare way: a formal proof containing 175,187 Lean modules and approximately 17 million lines of code.

Such a massive proof is difficult for mathematicians to review line by line. But computers can check it.

The independent verification log published by MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland shows that all 175,187 modules were successfully compiled, exporting 61.6GB of raw proof data. One independent checker, nanoda, ran on 80 threads for 27 minutes and 42 seconds and accepted the complete proof. Other independent checkers yielded the same result. Following traditional mathematical research methods, the proof of a major conjecture typically involves several stages: Researchers first publish the complete proof; experts in the relevant field then progressively examine the definitions, premises, and derivations, looking for potential flaws and attempting independent verification. Only through academic publication, peer review, and continuous testing does a consensus gradually form within the mathematical community. For the Riemann Hypothesis, there is a more explicit formal recognition procedure. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute listed it as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, offering a $1 million reward. According to the institute's revised rules in 2018, a solution must be published in a qualified academic publication, and after at least two years, and with widespread acceptance from the global mathematics community, the institute will consider initiating a formal evaluation. So, what did Lean accomplish this time? The most important step was to conduct a rigorous logical check on the entire formal proof and, through independent verification, confirm that it indeed proves the Riemann Hypothesis. This is equivalent to transforming the derivation process, which traditionally requires mathematicians to invest a great deal of effort in checking, into a verification task that computers can repeatedly execute. However, the mathematical ideas behind the proof still require human understanding, academic publication, broader peer discussion, and formal verification by the Clay Mathematics Institute. When AI can generate 17 million lines of mathematical proof, the traditional review method relying on experts reading page by page is difficult to keep up with such a scale. Why was Lean able to accomplish this task? How reliable are its verification results? These questions also become important entry points for understanding how AI research will establish credibility in the future.

Figure: The Riemann Hypothesis states that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line where the real part is 1/2. The figure marks the positions of some known zeros. A finite number of zeros satisfying this rule is not sufficient to prove that all zeros satisfy it.

How can Lean verify 17 million lines of proof?

Lean is not an intelligent agent, nor does it possess the autonomous exploration capabilities of Claude.

It is an open-source programming language and also a formal proof system. One of its main creators, Leonardo de Moura, has long been engaged in research on automated theorem proving. Image: Screenshot of actual code from a public presentation by the creator of Lean. The left side shows the formal proof, which can be checked by Lean after the proof script is run. Source: de Moura's presentation "Lean: How AI and Proof Automation Are Changing Mathematics". The technical foundation of Lean relies on type theory and the Curry-Howard correspondence in computer science. Simply put, mathematical propositions can be represented as types, and mathematical proofs are represented as objects belonging to that type. For example, to prove "If A is true, then A is true," in Lean, it can be written as a function that accepts a proof that A is true and returns that proof. Complex mathematical derivations follow similar principles. A proof may involve numerous definitions, lemmas, and intermediate conclusions, but ultimately must form a proof object that conforms to logical rules, which is then type-checked by the Lean kernel. This also explains the division of labor between Claude and Lean. Claude can continuously try different proof paths, overturn previous derivations, and reorganize mathematical proofs. Lean will check whether the final submitted proof is valid according to predetermined rules. Finding a proof and checking a proof are two different computational tasks. The former may require a huge search space and complex reasoning ability; the latter can usually be completed by a relatively concise program. Lean utilizes this to make large proofs repeatable. But here's another question: what exactly does the computer check? On November 12th, Imperial College London mathematician Kevin Buzzard published an article discussing what it really means for a study to claim it has been "verified by Lean." He points out that for a formal proof to pass the check, it must first confirm that the mathematical proposition being proven is consistent with the proposition the researcher originally intended to prove. For example, when formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem in a computer, if the correct constraints on the range of variable values ​​are omitted, a proposition inconsistent with the original theorem may be obtained. Even if a formal proof is subsequently submitted, it cannot be claimed that the original theorem has been verified. Therefore, the Lean community did not stop at simply ensuring the code compiled successfully. They first checked the formal definition of the Riemann Hypothesis. This definition comes from Mathlib, an open-source mathematical knowledge base maintained by mathematicians and developers, and has already been reviewed by experts in the relevant field. Subsequently, the community used independent tools to compare Alpöge's actual proof with the original definition in Mathlib, confirming their consistency. Finally, the proof was reviewed by multiple checkers, including the official Lean kernel, con-leche, and con-ron, and the axioms upon which the proof relies were also examined. However, even with such rigorous verification steps, Lean itself has had serious vulnerabilities. On July 25th of this year, researcher Ramana Kumar published a so-called "proof against" of the Collatz conjecture, completed using AI. This code did not use the "sorry" placeholder in Lean to indicate that the proof was incomplete, but successfully exploited a vulnerability in the kernel's handling of nested inductive types. Even more surprisingly, a separately implemented Rust checker, nanoda, also accepted this erroneous proof due to another software flaw. Subsequently, OpenAI researcher Daniel Selsam continued testing Lean using an internal AI model, discovering multiple logical kernel and runtime vulnerabilities between July and August. Some of these vulnerabilities could cause the system to incorrectly accept proofs of the logical proposition False. Lean creator de Moura publicly reviewed these issues in August and has since fixed them. This illustrates that while the logical rules upon which formal verification relies can be very strict, the software executing these rules can still err. Especially when AI can actively seek out vulnerabilities, the reliability of the checkers themselves is also tested. On October 15th, de Moura announced that Lean officially provides a new verification mechanism, including multiple independent checkers and a kernel implementation with formal reliability proofs. The reliability proof of con-leche is based on a set-theoretic model. It provides stronger guarantees against a class of kernel implementation errors, but still relies on the consistency of the corresponding mathematical foundations. The Riemann Hypothesis verification in November was completed using this continuously improving mechanism. The Lean community exports the proof as independent data and then uses checkers from different implementations to verify it, minimizing the impact of a single software defect on the final conclusion. This independent checking is particularly important for a proof of 17 million lines completed with AI participation. Lean demonstrates a research verification method that is already practically operational: the system generating the proof can be very complex, while the procedure for checking the proof can be relatively streamlined and can be independently verified by others. After 6.3 million lines of proof, who will check the remaining 27,000 lines? Formal verification is not a new technology. For decades, mathematicians and software engineers have been trying to use rigorous mathematical methods to prove that computer programs meet specific requirements. However, this technology has not been widely adopted in the general software industry, largely due to cost. For example, the well-known seL4 microkernel project initially required approximately 20 person-years for formal verification. Engineers needed to describe the program's behavior into precise mathematical specifications and then write numerous proofs to ensure the program met these specifications. For aerospace, cryptography, and safety-critical systems, such an investment might be worthwhile. But for most commercial software, building a dedicated formal verification team is impractical. AI is beginning to change the most human-intensive parts of this process. On November 10th, Google DeepMind announced its AlphaProof Code research, revealing that it has used an AI agent to formally verify the key security properties of libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal communication protocol. The research delves directly into the compiled AArch64 machine code, covering the specific version's cryptographic handshake and key update process. The team consists of five researchers, and the main proof work lasted four weeks. The AI ​​agent generated approximately 6.3 million lines of Lean proof code, which were ultimately checked by the Lean kernel. Perhaps the most noteworthy figure in this project is the additional 27,000 lines of code. Image: The verification process of AlphaProof Code. Researchers and AI jointly develop and review the Lean specification. The AI ​​proof team is responsible for generating the proof, which is ultimately checked by the Lean kernel and independent checkpoints. The verification results still rely on manually approved specifications and trusted execution models. According to DeepMind's online technical report, the 6.3 million lines of proof rely on approximately 19,000 lines of trusted formal definitions and approximately 8,000 lines of AArch64 machine code semantics. In addition, the research also relies on cryptographic assumptions, specific execution environment models, the reliability of compilation artifacts, and the verification tools themselves. The Trusted Computing Base (TCB) refers to the components and assumptions upon which a verification conclusion depends. AI can automatically generate millions of lines of proof, but what these proofs actually guarantee still depends on how humans define the verification objective. The DeepMind research team wrote in their report, "When proofs become cheap, the difficult problem shifts to what should be proven." They spend most of their effort on designing and verifying formal specifications. The underlying issue can be explained with a simple example. Suppose a financial institution requires AI to prove the security of its payment system. If the formal specification only requires that the account balance cannot be negative, then even if Lean successfully proves this property, it cannot rule out duplicate charges, unauthorized transfers, or user information leaks. DeepMind also disclosed a more extreme example. In a previous multi-agent proof task, one agent redefined the predicate used in a certain conjectural premise as False. Other agents subsequently adopted this modification. According to formal logic, if a premise is never true, then the implied propositions derived from that premise may be easily proven. The resulting proof may be formally valid, but it does not solve the original problem. This phenomenon does not necessarily mean that the AI ​​intentionally deceived. As long as AI is continuously pressured to complete tasks, it may reduce the difficulty of proof by adding constraints, narrowing the scope of application, or changing definitions. To avoid similar issues affecting the Signal project, DeepMind designed independent verification checkpoints. The proof agent cannot arbitrarily modify approved specifications; modifications involving credible assumptions require review. The final proof must be re-examined in a new environment and cannot rely on the agent reporting task success itself. The research team also reintroduced two previously patched Signal vulnerabilities into the program to test whether the formal specifications could identify these errors. This differs from ordinary software testing. Testing typically checks whether the program produces errors under selected inputs. Formal verification attempts to prove that, within a defined model and assumptions, all relevant behaviors of a program satisfy specified properties. However, the effectiveness of the latter ultimately depends on whether the specification is sufficiently complete and whether the model accurately describes the program being checked. The involvement of AI has made this previously extremely costly technology more economical. However, DeepMind's research is insufficient to prove that formal verification is universally commercially viable. The four weeks of work did not fully disclose the costs of model calls, computing power expenditures, and the previous tool development. Proving specific security properties does not mean that the entire Signal application is secure in all environments. At least for now, highly reliable software is likely to be the first area to benefit. As Coding Agents enter enterprises, the deliverables of some key software in the future may increase from code and test reports to code, formal specifications, and independently verifiable proofs of correctness. The truly difficult work may increasingly focus on accurately describing the requirements that the system should meet. Having verified the mathematical logic, who will verify the real world? Lean provides a rigorous checking mechanism for AI-generated mathematical proofs, but the verification problem in scientific research is far more complex than mathematical theorems. Mathematical proofs derive conclusions under clear definitions, axioms, and logical rules. Research in physics, chemistry, biology, and other fields must also verify whether the assumptions in the model conform to reality and whether theoretical predictions can be confirmed by experiments and observations. A mathematical model may be perfectly self-consistent, yet it may fail to accurately describe the real world. This problem is particularly prevalent in the simulation of complex systems. On October 31st of this year, the *Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation* published a study attempting to combine the statistical model checking tool MultiVeStA with the multi-agent simulation platform NetLogo to improve the rigor of simulation result analysis. NetLogo, developed in 1999, is widely used to simulate interactions between large numbers of individuals, such as population migration, ecosystem evolution, and economic activities. Researchers can set different individual behavior rules and run the system hundreds or even thousands of times to observe the final changes in the population. This paper uses a model simulating population changes in an ancient Anasazi settlement in the southwestern United States, attempting to recreate population changes between 800 and 1350 AD. The research team tested 1600 parameter combinations and compared the simulation results with historical data. Following common methods, the set of parameters that best fits the historical population curve can be selected as the final result. However, after conducting statistical checks using MultiVeStA, the researchers found that, at the set precision, the fitting performance of 14 parameter combinations could not be statistically distinguished. This means that even if the best-performing parameter is found, it cannot be considered the only reliable explanation. Another experiment also illustrates the importance of the number of simulations. Previous studies used 15 independent simulations to estimate population changes, but during periods of high volatility, the confidence intervals were very wide, easily leading researchers to misjudge the model's consistency with historical data. MultiVeStA automatically adjusts the number of simulations based on statistical precision requirements. In some periods, 100 to 600 simulations are needed to obtain more reliable estimates. These results reveal a common risk in simulation science: If the number of experiments is insufficient or the parameter selection lacks statistical basis, researchers may have overly high confidence in the model's interpretive power.

Figure: Increasing the number of simulations changes researchers' judgment of the results. Statistical checks on the NetLogo population model show that performing only 15 simulations may not accurately determine the differences between the model and historical data in some periods. MultiVeStA narrows the uncertainty of the estimate by adaptively increasing the number of simulations.

Lean can rigorously check the logical derivation of formal propositions. NetLogo provides a simulation environment for complex systems, and MultiVeStA can help researchers analyze simulation outputs more reliably under specified statistical conditions.

Different stages of scientific research require different validation methods. For mathematical propositions, researchers can use tools like Lean to check proofs. For software systems, this verifies whether the program meets explicit functional and safety specifications. For stochastic simulations, parameter uncertainty, the number of experiments, and statistical errors need to be considered. For natural science hypotheses, ultimately, real experiments and observations are needed to determine whether the theory matches reality. These methods can establish varying degrees of credible evidence, but they cannot completely replace each other. This is also a real problem facing AI for Science. AI has already been able to participate in mathematical proofs, scientific model building, research hypothesis generation, and experimental design. However, the increasing number of AI-generated results does not mean that every result can be directly verified by a formal checker like a mathematical theorem. Some results can be confirmed through rigorous logical deduction, some require large-scale numerical experiments, and some must be verified through expensive real-world experiments. Therefore, the future of AI research not only requires stronger models but also verification tools that can be matched with different research tasks, as well as traceable definitions, data, code, proofs, and experimental records. Lean has demonstrated an important possibility: as the cost of AI-generated proofs decreases, formal verification work that previously relied heavily on expert labor can be automated to some extent. However, this also exposes another problem: if AI can generate tens of millions of lines of mathematical proof in a short time, how much effort will mathematicians need to invest in understanding the ideas behind the proof? When AI further participates in biological, materials, and physics research, how many experiments and how much data will be needed to determine if a discovery has genuine scientific value? How exactly should silicon-based intelligence and carbon-based intelligence cooperate to properly unlock new frontiers of scientific discovery? This is a technical question, but even more so, a philosophical one.

data.title: Cracks Appear in the AI ​​Narrative, Global Risk Assets Under Pressure
data.description:
Author: Zhou Hao, Chief Economist at GTJAI, Guotai Haitong Securities

Over the past week, global markets continued the main logic of the past few months: relatively robust US growth, a hawkish stance maintained by the Federal Reserve, and continued support for dollar assets. However, at the same time, some noteworthy new changes have begun to emerge in the market. The relative advantage of the US economy remains, but has not expanded further; the dollar remains in a strong range, but its upward momentum has slowed; and the AI ​​narrative supporting global risk appetite has encountered its first significant test of volatility.

Economic data has further reinforced that the US remains the most resilient economy among major economies. Although October retail sales slowed to 0.2% from 0.8% in the previous month, the core control group, which better reflects actual consumer demand, grew by 0.6%, significantly better than expected, indicating that consumer spending remains resilient as the year-end shopping season approaches.

Meanwhile, the labor market showed signs of marginal cooling, with the number of people continuing to receive unemployment benefits rising to 1.763 million, a recent high; the housing market continued to be under pressure, with the homebuyer confidence index falling to a 14-year low and pending home sales hitting a record low. Leading economic indicators continued to decline, also indicating that economic momentum is slowly weakening. These data do not reflect a one-sided strength or weakness in the economy, but rather a divergence in the growth structure. Consumption can still support overall demand, but interest rate-sensitive sectors continue to be under pressure; the job market has not yet shown substantial deterioration, but signs of slowdown are gradually accumulating. For the Federal Reserve, this means that growth is not weak enough to support a policy shift, and the inflationary environment makes maintaining a restrictive interest rate a relatively reasonable option. This is also reflected in the statements made by several Federal Reserve officials last week. Whether discussing overly loose financial conditions, persistent inflationary pressures, or the possibility of further interest rate hikes, the overall tone points to the same thing: monetary policy is unlikely to see a significant shift until there is clearer progress in curbing inflation. This has suppressed market optimism regarding a rate-cutting path in 2027. From an asset pricing perspective, the core of market trading over the past few months has not been the absolute strength of the US economy, but rather the US's advantage relative to Europe, Japan, and other major economies. Europe is experiencing stagnant growth and rising fiscal constraints, Japan is still in the early stages of policy normalization, and some Asian economies are affected by the technology cycle and slowing global demand. Against this backdrop, US assets remain the most concentrated destination for global capital. However, it's important to note that this relative advantage has already been largely reflected in prices. The US dollar index has been rising steadily over the past few months, while the euro has fallen to near an 18-month low, with short positions in the euro reaching extreme levels in recent years. Institutions such as Deutsche Bank have further raised their future dollar forecasts, essentially betting that high US real interest rates and the AI ​​investment cycle will continue to attract global capital inflows. However, as market consensus becomes more concentrated, prices tend to become less sensitive to new positive news. The market performance over the past week has already demonstrated this characteristic. Despite generally strong US data and a hawkish stance from Federal Reserve officials, the dollar failed to extend its gains further. Instead, during Friday's correction in the technology sector, funds flowed more into traditional safe-haven assets such as the yen and Swiss franc. The dollar remains in a strong range, but its status as the sole safe-haven asset has not been further strengthened. The performance of the yen is particularly noteworthy. Despite speculative funds maintaining significant short positions in the yen, it became the best-performing G10 currency last week. The market is beginning to reassess the potential for a sustained one-sided rise in the USD/JPY exchange rate, especially given the increasing signs of a marginal slowdown in the US economy. This doesn't mean the dollar cycle is over, but it does indicate a more cautious market expectation of continued dollar appreciation. More noteworthy changes last week than the macroeconomic data itself came from the market narrative. Over the past year, AI has become arguably the most important variable in global asset pricing. The expansion of US tech stock valuations, the sustained high US real interest rates, and the continued strength of the dollar have all benefited to varying degrees from the capital expenditure wave and increased growth expectations brought about by AI. Therefore, AI is not only an industry theme but also a crucial component supporting the American exceptionalism narrative. However, last week the US further tightened restrictions on AI chip exports, triggering turmoil in related Asian supply chains, and the pullback in the US tech sector prompted the market to reassess the valuation levels of AI trades. Currently, this appears more like a position adjustment than a reversal of logic. Neither capital expenditure trends nor corporate investment directions have fundamentally changed. But the market is beginning to raise new questions: will the continued rise in asset prices be driven by the expansion of AI itself, or by the expansion of investor expectations for AI? There is a fundamental difference between the two. Over the past year, the market has traded more on expectations; as valuations continue to rise, the market needs to see more concrete profit realization, clearer productivity improvements, and more sustainable capital returns. This applies to US tech stocks as well as the US dollar. Therefore, the signals released by the market last week were neither a disappearance of the US advantage nor a reversal of global risk appetite. More accurately, the US economy, the dollar, and AI-related assets still dominate the market, but the logic driving their rise has gradually shifted from "constantly being validated" to "needing continuous validation." Looking ahead to this week, market focus will return to the data level. The US core PCE, European and American PMIs, and Tokyo CPI will be important observation windows. If US inflation continues to show stickiness, the Fed's rationale for maintaining high interest rates will be further strengthened; if signs of slowing growth continue to accumulate, then market attention may gradually shift from "why the US is stronger than other economies" to "how long can this advantage be maintained?" For global investors, this may be the most important question in the market right now. It's not surprising that US assets have outperformed global markets over the past year; what's truly noteworthy is where the next wave of market-driving information will come from, now that this expectation has been largely priced in.

data.title: The Riemann Hypothesis has been proven. Is the pie still safe?
data.description: A few days ago, the mathematics community achieved a major breakthrough in a century-old problem. On November 20, 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that, with the help of the artificial intelligence Claude, he had completed a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and published approximately 17 million lines of Lean code. This is of great significance, as the Riemann Hypothesis is listed as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in Mathematics by the Clay Mathematics Institute, and numerous papers and theories are based on the premise that the Riemann Hypothesis is true. However, to be cautious, as of November 23, 2026, the Clay Mathematics Institute website still lists the Riemann Hypothesis as an unsolved problem. While significant progress has been made in the formal verification of the mathematical proof, the academic community's in-depth understanding of the proof's approach, and the formal review of the Millennium Prize, still have their respective procedures. Therefore, let's wait and see, everyone, and remain calm. But many marketing accounts are starting to use headlines like "The Riemann Hypothesis Proved, Bitcoin in Danger" to scare people. Frankly, I have absolutely no interest in opening them, but many members have privately messaged me asking if this matter really has any impact. To help you avoid the stress of investing, I'll explain it in the most roundabout way possible. Of course, let me clarify: I'm neither a mathematician nor a cryptographer. I simply believe that if something cannot be verified, it shouldn't be taken as imminent. Many marketing accounts may not even understand what the Riemann Hypothesis is, so let's start with a brief discussion. I also encourage you to find relevant videos to supplement your understanding with more details. Let's begin with a simple question. What do the numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 have in common? Answer: They are all prime numbers. A prime number is a positive integer that is divisible only by 1 and itself. For example, the number 7 mentioned above is divisible only by 1 and 7, and cannot be multiplied by two smaller integers. Prime numbers seem ordinary, but they hold a very special place in the world of mathematics. You can think of prime numbers as the basic building blocks of the integer world; almost all integers greater than 1 can be broken down into the product of several prime numbers. For example, 12 can be broken down into 2 multiplied by 2 and then multiplied by 3, and 30 can be broken down into 2 multiplied by 3 and then multiplied by 5. In principle, every number, regardless of its size, can be factored into a prime number. This is crucial because prime numbers form the foundation of integer multiplication. However, this also presents a problem. What patterns govern the occurrence of prime numbers? Starting from 2, prime numbers seem relatively concentrated. As the number increases, the frequency of prime numbers decreases. Within a long range of numbers, you might encounter many prime numbers, or you might encounter only one after a long time. These patterns appear regular, yet it's difficult to find a simple one. Therefore, mathematicians are determined to find a method or pattern. They want to understand how prime numbers are distributed as numbers continue to increase. Can we estimate in advance how many prime numbers will appear before a certain huge number? This leads to the Prime Number Theorem, which, simply put, gives the average distribution pattern of prime numbers. It helps mathematicians estimate the approximate number of prime numbers within a large range, but this is not enough. We know the average trend, but we still don't know how much the actual distribution will deviate from this trend. Let's try to understand this with a real-life example. If you know that a city's average annual rainfall is 900 millimeters, then you know where the minimum flood control line for building a reservoir is, and you can then establish a reasonable reservoir height. However, for you personally, whether you need to bring an umbrella tomorrow, this 900 millimeters of average rainfall is meaningless. Therefore, the prime number theorem provides an annual average value, while the Riemann Hypothesis aims to answer the question of the range of fluctuation. And as mentioned earlier, Riemann himself didn't claim to have proven it; he only wrote "very likely," and then used this assumption as a ladder to derive a series of conclusions. In summary, the Riemann Hypothesis essentially sets a very precise constraint on the distribution of prime numbers, allowing mathematicians to further understand the extent of the deviation between the actual distribution of prime numbers and the average distribution. Why is it so important? Because prime numbers permeate almost the entire system of number theory. From integer factorization to various number-theoretic functions, and even modern cryptography, much mathematical research relies on prime numbers. If the Riemann Hypothesis holds true, it means that mathematicians can more accurately grasp a series of conclusions related to the distribution of prime numbers. So, after all that rambling, many of you are probably getting impatient, practically ready to grab my hand through the internet and yell: Will this affect the security of BigPie?! I know you're anxious, but hold on a second. We've just been discussing data science, while BigPie is about cryptography, which you can think of as a set of mathematical rules. BigPie's set of rules needs to solve one problem: how to allow others to verify your right to use a certain asset, while simultaneously preventing them from deducing the secrets you possess based solely on publicly available information. This is the value of BigPie's system, and the "core" that supports BigPie's future. The two most crucial concepts here are the private key and the public key. You can think of a private key as a key that only you possess, while the public key is a publicly available piece of information generated through mathematical operations. A wallet uses the private key to generate a public key. Others who know your public key can verify transactions you've signed, but they cannot easily deduce the private key from the public key. The elliptic curve cryptography used by Bitcoin primarily relies on a mathematical problem called the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. The name sounds complicated, but it can actually be understood through a simple process: Imagine you have a secret number. Following a specific set of rules, you can easily derive another public number. Calculating the public number from the secret number is fast. However, conversely, knowing only the public number and trying to find the original secret number using current classical methods requires an extremely high computational cost. This is the basic idea behind elliptic curve cryptography. Bitcoin uses a curve called secp256k1. The equation is very simple; all operations are performed within a range defined by a 256-bit prime number. The private key is a large integer, and the public key is obtained by multiplying the private key by a fixed point: Q = d × G. Simply put, all related calculations are performed according to a fixed mathematical rule, and the result is restricted to a definite range. Don't be fooled by the simple formula and explanation; the multiplication here isn't ordinary multiplication. It involves repeatedly adding the fixed point G along the curve d times. Using a doubling technique, the computer can calculate the public key from a 256-bit private key in a few hundred operations—negligible speed. Furthermore, note that this prime number is extremely large, with a size of 256 bits. So, if we're not in a panic, we should rationally ask: Since the mathematical tools used by PieCard are related to prime numbers, will the distribution patterns of prime numbers studied by the Riemann Hypothesis affect the security of elliptic curve cryptography? Again, I know you're in a hurry, but don't rush, because we need to understand another important technology of PieCard. Regarding encryption, PieCard uses two locks; we just discussed the first lock, and now we're moving on to the second. This is SHA-256. If elliptic curve cryptography is primarily responsible for transaction authorization, then SHA-256 in the Pie network handles tasks including hash calculation, blockchain integration, and proof-of-work, such as the familiar mining: Miners need to continuously modify the data in the block header, repeatedly calculating the hash value until they find a result that meets the network difficulty requirements. This process uses double SHA-256. A hash algorithm has a very interesting characteristic: a slight change in the input data can result in a completely different hash result. You can think of it as a special kind of digital mixer; whether the input is a sentence, an image, or an entire block, it can produce a fixed-length result. Deducing the original data from this result is computationally very difficult. Here's an interesting detail to add.
