The SHA-256 algorithm does use numbers related to prime numbers as some initial constants during its design. These numbers come from the decimal parts of the square and cube roots of the first few prime numbers, which seems to have some connection to the Riemann Hypothesis. However, these are merely fixed numbers chosen during the algorithm's design. SHA-256 does not require the Riemann Hypothesis to function, and its security does not depend on whether the Riemann Hypothesis is true. Therefore, we now know that the security system of Pie involves two important tools: Elliptic curve cryptography, used for key and transaction authorization; and the SHA-256 hash algorithm, used for data integrity, blockchain connectivity, and proof-of-work. They address different problems. So, back to the initial title: The Riemann Hypothesis has been proven, is the Pie chart still safe? The answer is somewhat unexpected. While there is indeed a mathematical connection between the two, it's not as direct as one might imagine. The Riemann Hypothesis studies the distribution of prime numbers throughout the sequence of natural numbers. One uses prime numbers, the other studies prime numbers. It seems like there's a deep connection. But there's a crucial difference: the Pie chart uses elliptic curves, requiring only a single, determined prime number and a set of designed and verified mathematical rules. It doesn't need to know how all prime numbers will be distributed in the future, nor does it need to rely on the Riemann Hypothesis to determine a prime number. The difference between the two is somewhat like not classifying nail trimming as a surgical procedure, although it might seem somewhat related. Therefore, you can remember this: BigPie's cryptography uses mathematical tools related to prime numbers, but its security is not based on the premise that the Riemann Hypothesis is true. Or, from a discussion perspective, what would happen to BigPie if the Riemann Hypothesis were formally proven, or one day disproven? First, let's assume the Riemann Hypothesis is eventually proven true. This means mathematicians will have a more solid theoretical foundation for understanding the distribution of prime numbers, leading to significant progress in mathematical research and potentially further refining algorithmic analysis that relies on related number theory conclusions. However, for Pie, this won't automatically grant it greater security. Your private key won't become longer, your public key won't change, and SHA-256 won't suddenly become more secure because the Riemann Hypothesis is proven. Pie's existing consensus rules, cryptographic parameters, and transaction verification methods won't automatically change because of this mathematical proof. So, what if the situation were reversed? Suppose that mathematicians eventually discover that the Riemann Hypothesis is wrong, finding a counterexample that does not conform to the original conjecture. This would indeed be a major event in the history of mathematics. Many theoretical conclusions relying on the Riemann Hypothesis would need to be re-examined, and the research directions of some mathematicians might change as a result. However, this still does not directly lead to the conclusion that the cryptographic system of the Riemann Hypothesis has been compromised, because proving the Riemann Hypothesis is wrong and finding an algorithm that can quickly solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem are two different things. Only when subsequent research discovers a new, exploitable algorithm that can effectively attack existing cryptographic systems under realistic computational conditions will a real security threat be posed. As of now, progress in proving the Riemann Hypothesis has not yielded such a conclusion. Therefore, whether the Riemann Hypothesis is proven true or ultimately disproven, we cannot conclude that Pyramid's security will change based solely on this one event. I've written a bit too much, so let me end with a reminder: whether you're a veteran in the crypto space like me since 2017, or a newbie who's just entered the field, you need to understand that cryptographic security and asset management security are two issues that need to be considered separately. Looking back, the Riemann Hypothesis remains an extremely important mathematical problem, studying the patterns behind prime numbers and helping humanity further understand the digital world. The Pie, on the other hand, is a system that combines mathematics, cryptography, computer networks, and economic incentives. There is mathematical overlap between the two, but they also have their own independent research problems. We should certainly pay attention to advancements in mathematics and technology, especially breakthroughs that may change the existing boundaries of cryptographic security. However, there's no need to worry about whether your wallet will be able to open tomorrow just because a mathematical problem has been solved. Understanding the boundaries of technology is far more important than panicking at the sound of a new term. Please verify, do not believe. This statement applies to investing, and it also applies to the technical field. 1 BTC = 1 BTC. At least today, the progress in proving the Riemann Hypothesis has not changed this. Security should come from understanding the hypothesis, not from associations with its name. Wishing everyone a good mindset to navigate through cycles.

data.title: Chainflip Confirms $12 Million Crypto Hack After Bitcoin and Ethereum Vaults Are Drained, Offers Hacker $1.2 Million to Return Stolen Funds
data.description:
Chainflip is offering an attacker a $1.2 million reward to return most of the $12 million stolen from its cross-chain vaults, as the protocol attempts to recover funds and limit further damage following the exploit.

The attacker has until 18:38 UTC on 23 November 2026 to return 90% of the stolen assets, with Chainflip promising to allow the hacker to keep the remaining 10% as a bounty.

The company said it would classify the incident as a white-hat recovery and withdraw its law enforcement complaints if the funds were returned before the deadline.

We have sent an on-chain message to the address holding the BTC taken from Chainflip on 21 November.

Offer: return 90% of the funds, keep 10% as a bounty. Terms and return addresses: https://t.co/hspHwh43lw

Tx: https://t.co/NrYEeZFMxD

The offer is open until 18:38 UTC on 23…

— CHAINFLIP (@Chainflip) November 21, 2026

Chainflip Confirms $12 Million Loss Across Bitcoin, Ethereum and Stablecoin Vaults

Chainflip Labs, the operator of the cross-chain decentralised exchange, confirmed that attackers stole 122.86 Bitcoin (BTC), 520.22 Ether (ETH), 3.25 million USDC and 758,141 USDT in the 21 November 2026 incident.

The confirmed losses are substantially higher than the initial estimate of $4.86 million, which covered assets drained from an Ethereum vault.

Chainflip (@Chainflip) was hacked for 4.86M!

Thestolenfundsinclude3.25MUSDC, 520.22 ETH(851K), and 758K USDT.

Thehackerhasalreadyswappedallthestolenfundsfor2,910ETH (4.76M)anddepositedtheETH into #TornadoCash.https://t.co/ZzOMJZaY8F… pic.twitter.com/d0ooM4uhxp

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) November 21, 2026

Further investigations uncovered another $7.1 million in Bitcoin stolen from a separate Bitcoin vault, bringing the total losses to approximately $12 million.

The scale of the incident is particularly concerning given the protocol's relatively small reserves.

According to DeFiLlama, Chainflip's total value locked (TVL) stood at approximately $14.45 million a week before the attack, meaning the stolen assets represented more than 80% of that figure.

Chainflip's native FLIP token also suffered heavy losses following the incident.

According to CoinGecko data, the token fell as much as 42.9% over 24 hours, while subsequent reports placed its decline at around 37%.

How Did the Attacker Gain Access to Chainflip's Vaults?

Chainflip traced preparations for the attack to 11 November, when the attacker allegedly funded activity through Tornado Cash, followed by a FLIP token purchase and the registration of a validator account on 20 November.

According to DeFiLlama's hack database, the attacker exploited Chainflip's aggregate validator signing key by using a valid Schnorr signature with an unusual nonce outside the protocol's normal signing sequence.

This enabled the attacker to drain assets from the Ethereum vault.

The stolen stablecoins were subsequently converted into Ether, with approximately 2,909 ETH transferred to Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service used to obscure transaction trails.

CHAINFLIP HIT BY 4.86MEXPLOIT,HACKERLAUNDERSETHTHROUGHTORNADOCASH

Anattackerdrained520.2ETH, 3.25M USDC and 758K USDT (~$4.86M) from Chainflip's Ethereum vault.

The exploit involved a valid signature from the vault's aggregate signing key, suggesting a private key… pic.twitter.com/F8qxDULnax

— Onchain Lens (@OnchainLens) November 21, 2026

Chainflip has since identified the mechanism behind the cryptographic key exposure and said it had taken steps to prevent similar incidents.

However, the exact technical details of the vulnerability have not been fully disclosed.

The protocol's security structure relies on validators jointly managing a signing key.

Its system can involve up to 150 validators, with at least 100 required to approve transactions, making the potential compromise of its shared signing infrastructure a central concern.

A valid signature is not a safe transaction.

Chainflip paid out on a signature that matched the live key but carried an out-of-sequence nonce. The check passed. The vault still emptied.

Verifying who signed is not enough. Something has to check what is being signed (nonce,…

— 0xki (@W3B_AI_SR) November 23, 2026

Chainflip Warns Attacker as It Offers 10% Bounty

Alongside its investigation, Chainflip issued a direct message to the attacker, offering to treat the return of 90% of the stolen assets as a white-hat recovery rather than pursuing the individual through law enforcement.

The company set the deadline at 18:38 UTC on 23 November, offering the attacker approximately $1.2 million worth of assets in exchange for returning the remaining funds.

Chainflip also identified the wallets designated to receive the recovered Bitcoin and Ether, which correspond to the safe-return addresses listed in its bug bounty policy.

The company warned that it had obtained identifying information connected to the validator and servers involved in the attack, while the associated wallet addresses had been flagged by major blockchain analytics firms.

Chainflip said,

“We hold identifying information on the validator and servers used, your addresses are flagged across every major analytics firm, and every Tornado Cash withdrawal is being watched.”

The company added that it would withdraw its reports and complaints to law enforcement if the attacker met the recovery conditions before the deadline.

Service Remains Suspended as Chainflip Reviews Compensation

Chainflip has suspended its service following the exploit while it works to secure its infrastructure and investigate the full extent of the damage.

Founder Simon Harman said he is cooperating with law enforcement and investigators, while acknowledging the financial impact on liquidity providers.

“Liquidity providers have suffered substantial losses, but I am relatively confident that we will be able to resume the service.”

Quick update on the @Chainflip situation: I've been in contact with all of our stakeholders, team, and external law enforcement and investigative organisations since the incident yesterday and we've all been working hard to do what needs to be done in the immediate aftermath.…

— Simon Harman 🫵 (@SimonAHarman) November 22, 2026

The company is also reviewing possible compensation arrangements for affected liquidity providers as it assesses the damage and considers how to restore operations.

Although Chainflip has identified the mechanism behind the attack and secured information that could help investigators trace the attacker, the recovery of the stolen assets remains uncertain.

data.title: Hong Kong CARF Launch: Tighter Taxation for Crypto Enthusiasts – Are There Risks in Withdrawing Funds for Crypto Trading?
data.description:
Hong Kong is advancing its Crypto Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), planning to collect crypto asset transaction information starting in 2027 and launch related reporting and cross-border information exchange in 2028. This news has sparked widespread discussion in the Chinese crypto community, even triggering some panic. This episode of "Wu Says No Crypto" invites FinTax founder Calix to explain the differences between CARF and traditional CRS and exchange KYC, and how the new regulations will affect Hong Kong and overseas exchanges, crypto investors, and Web3 practitioners. Calix points out that the core of CARF is to allow different tax jurisdictions to exchange crypto asset transaction information, and the reporting obligation does not entirely depend on whether the exchange is licensed or registered in which country. Regarding the tax issues that investors are most concerned about, Calix explained that although transactions before 2027 are not within the scope of the first round of transaction information collection by Hong Kong CARF, this does not mean that historical assets and income are automatically exempt from tax audits. Crypto assets accumulated before 2027 may still be subject to reporting when transferred or exchanged after 2027. Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax, but crypto assets obtained through business activities or remuneration may still be subject to profits tax or salaries tax. For individuals who have moved from mainland China to Hong Kong, obtaining Hong Kong residency does not automatically mean losing mainland tax residency; specific tax obligations still depend on the actual circumstances. The interview also discussed the impact of mainland China not yet joining CARF, whether cryptocurrency withdrawals through Hong Kong bank cards will leave tax records, and whether historical income may be retroactively pursued in the future. Calix believes that even if crypto transaction information is not yet exchanged with mainland China through CARF, Hong Kong bank accounts may still be subject to CRS information exchange. However, there is still uncertainty regarding mainland China's crypto asset tax rules, the scope of future audits, and the retrospective period. He suggests that Web3 practitioners and high-net-worth investors should proactively review their asset sources, transaction records, and tax residency status, rather than waiting until regulations are implemented to address historical issues. What are the differences between CARF, CRS, and KYC? What information do investors need to declare? AKI: Hong Kong plans to start collecting crypto asset transaction information from 2027. What exactly is CARF? How does it differ from traditional CRS and exchange KYC? Calix: CARF (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework) can be understood as the CRS for the crypto asset field. It primarily targets qualified crypto asset service providers, namely RCASP (Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers). These institutions are required to collect user identity and transaction information and report it to the local tax authorities as required. The tax authorities then exchange information with other participating jurisdictions based on the user's tax residency status. While CRS mainly covers traditional financial accounts such as banks and securities firms, CARF extends information exchange to crypto asset transactions. KYC is the basic procedure for platforms to identify customers, while CARF further requires platforms to collect tax residency information and related transaction data, and to fulfill tax reporting obligations. AKI: What specific obligations are added for investors and trading platforms? Calix: Investors first need to provide the platform with self-verification of their tax residency. If there is a significant change in their residency, the platform is also responsible for re-verification. The platform then needs to combine KYC, tax residency information, and transaction records to complete the annual CARF report. For investors, the biggest change is that tax authorities may obtain their cryptocurrency transaction records through cross-border information exchange and further inquire about the source of assets, the nature of income, and tax payment status. It's important to note that CARF itself is not a new tax system, but rather an information collection and exchange mechanism. Whether or not taxes need to be paid, and at what tax rate, still depends on the existing tax laws of each region. Will CARF weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness in the crypto space? Will offshore exchanges be affected? AKI: Hong Kong has been actively developing its crypto industry in recent years. Will CARF weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness relative to financial centers like Singapore? Calix: I believe the impact will be limited. CARF is an international tax cooperation framework, and major financial centers are gradually establishing similar information exchange systems. The international tax transparency requirements faced by financial centers such as Hong Kong, Singapore, and London are not fundamentally different. For Hong Kong, participating in CARF means both providing relevant tax information to other regions and gaining access to the transaction records of Hong Kong tax residents on overseas platforms. In the long run, systems such as anti-money laundering, KYC, CRS, and CARF help improve the transparency of financial activities. I don't believe CARF will significantly weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness as a financial center. AKI: Does CARF only apply to licensed exchanges in Hong Kong? If an exchange is registered overseas, is it exempt from reporting? Calix: CARF and exchange licensing are two different systems. Whether reporting is required depends primarily on whether the institution meets the RCASP definition and complies with local Nexus Rules, not just whether it has a license. For example, a company registered in the BVI but with its actual management team, principal activities, or place of business located in Hong Kong may have sufficient tax connection with Hong Kong to incur CARF reporting obligations. For users, tax residency is equally important. If a Hong Kong tax resident trades on a European platform, their transaction information may be exchanged with Hong Kong through European tax authorities if relevant information exchange arrangements are in place there. Using a Hong Kong-based platform may also incur local reporting obligations. Therefore, it cannot be simply assumed that using offshore exchanges will avoid CARF. In the future, transaction information from different platforms may gradually be aggregated in the user's tax jurisdiction. Will transactions and positions before 2027 be retroactively taxed? AKI: Hong Kong plans to start collecting transaction information from 2027 and launch reporting and exchange in 2028. How will transactions and positions before that be handled? Calix: According to the currently discussed implementation arrangements, transactions occurring before 2027 are not within the scope of the first round of CARF transaction information collection. However, it's important to distinguish between historical transactions and historical assets. For example, if someone accumulated a large amount of BTC before 2027, these historical transactions themselves will not be automatically included in the first round of reporting due to the launch of CARF. However, if the relevant assets are transferred, exchanged, or sold after 2027, the new transactions may be included in the reporting scope. More importantly, CARF's non-retroactive collection of historical transactions does not mean that historical gains are automatically tax-exempt. If the tax authorities discover that an account has a large amount of historically accumulated crypto assets, they may still require an explanation of the source and acquisition method of the assets, as well as whether there was taxable income previously, based on existing tax laws. Therefore, 2027 is not a tax-related starting point for clearing or recalculating assets. Whether historical assets involve tax obligations depends on the applicable law at the time of acquisition. Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax; are cryptocurrency gains still taxable? AKI: Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax, so are investors exempt from taxing gains from trading crypto assets? Calix: It can't be generalized. Hong Kong doesn't have a capital gains tax, but it still has profits tax and salaries tax; the key is the nature of the income. If an individual holds crypto assets long-term, the proceeds from the sale are considered capital gains and usually don't involve capital gains tax. However, if the transaction constitutes a business transaction, the profits generated may fall under the scope of profits tax. The standard profits tax rate for Hong Kong corporations is 16.5%, but the actual applicable tax rate depends on the type of entity and relevant regulations. If an individual receives compensation in crypto assets through work, such as receiving wages in USDT or other tokens, they may be subject to salaries tax. Hong Kong does not simply determine taxation based on the length of time a position is held, but rather on the nature of the transaction, business activities, and source of income. AKI: How is this assessed for Web3 companies registered in the BVI or Cayman Islands but with their actual teams located in Hong Kong? Calix: It requires consideration of the company's tax residency, the location of its business activities, and CARF reporting obligations. If a company is registered in an offshore jurisdiction but its actual management and operations primarily take place in Hong Kong, it may have a tax relationship with Hong Kong. Especially for cryptocurrency asset service providers, whether they need to fulfill CARF reporting obligations in Hong Kong cannot be determined solely by their place of registration or whether they have obtained a Hong Kong license; it also requires consideration of the RCASP definition and the Nexus Rules. However, CARF reporting obligations and whether a company needs to pay Hong Kong profits tax are not the same issue and must be analyzed separately. Where should mainland residents pay taxes after relocating to Hong Kong? AKI: If a mainland resident obtains Hong Kong residency and lives in Hong Kong long-term, which tax law should govern the income from crypto assets before and after the relocation? Calix: First, it's necessary to determine the individual's tax residency status. Obtaining Hong Kong residency does not automatically mean losing mainland tax residency status. Mainland tax law determines resident individuals based on factors such as domicile and length of residence. Tax-specific domicile requires consideration of household registration, family, and economic interests. Therefore, even if someone lives in Hong Kong long-term, they may still retain mainland tax residency status and be subject to corresponding reporting obligations.

Specifically, there may be situations where taxes are only paid in Hong Kong, or where tax returns are filed in both Hong Kong and mainland China. If double taxation exists, it needs to be handled in conjunction with the applicable tax arrangements and credit rules.

For crypto assets, the issue is more complex.

For example, receiving wages in the form of crypto assets, obtaining tokens through business activities, or converting investment income into fiat currency via OTC may involve different tax classifications.

Currently, there is still uncertainty regarding the specific tax treatment of different types of crypto asset income in mainland China, and it cannot be simply assumed that all crypto investment income is uniformly subject to a 20% tax rate.

There is still uncertainty regarding the specific tax treatment of different types of crypto asset income in mainland China, and it cannot be simply assumed that all crypto investment income is uniformly subject to a 20% tax rate.

Therefore, assets and income before and after relocating to Hong Kong need to be assessed separately based on the time of acquisition, the nature of income, and the tax residency status in both locations. Will withdrawals from Hong Kong bank cards be detected by the tax authorities if mainland China has not yet joined CARF? AKI: Mainland China has not yet joined CARF. If a mainland tax resident trades crypto assets in Hong Kong, will the relevant information be exchanged with the mainland? Calix: According to the current CARF participation arrangements, mainland China has not yet joined this information exchange framework. Therefore, relevant crypto asset transaction information will not be directly exchanged with the mainland through the CARF mechanism for the time being. However, this does not mean that all overseas financial information cannot be obtained, because CARF and CRS are two different systems. AKI: If crypto is exchanged for fiat currency via OTC and then transferred to a Hong Kong bank card, is it possible for mainland tax authorities to detect this? Calix: This involves CRS. If the tax residency of the Hong Kong bank account holder is identified as mainland China, the relevant account information may be exchanged with mainland tax authorities in accordance with CRS rules. The information exchanged through CRS typically includes the account holder's identity, account balance or value, and specific income and related amounts, but it does not mean that banks will automatically provide details of every cryptocurrency transaction. However, if tax authorities obtain information about overseas accounts through CRS and find a significant discrepancy between the account's funds and declared income, they may further inquire about the source of the funds. Therefore, even if cryptocurrency transaction information is not currently exchanged through CARF, once funds enter the traditional banking system, records that can be used for tax audits may still remain. Will mainland China retroactively examine historical Crypto income in the future? AKI: If mainland China strengthens tax regulation of crypto assets in the future, is it possible to retroactively apply investment income from the past few years? Calix: I think this possibility cannot be ruled out, but the specific timing, scope, and method are currently impossible to determine. Crypto assets have accumulated considerable wealth, and related income may come from investment, mining, staking, DeFi, token issuance, or other business activities. These activities may have different tax implications, and some may be subject to existing tax laws. Future regulation may first clarify the tax treatment of different crypto asset income through departmental regulations or policy interpretations, and then gradually improve the legal system. However, whether historical gains should be retroactively investigated, for how many years, and how to distinguish between ordinary underreporting and tax evasion all require specific legal provisions and cannot be concluded in advance. AKI: Which investors are likely to be the first to be audited by the tax authorities? Will they be screened based on asset size or trading frequency? Calix: It is currently impossible to make a reliable judgment. There are still many unclear aspects in the tax rules and actual collection methods for crypto assets in mainland China, and it is impossible to simply speculate that large investors, high-frequency traders, or certain types of practitioners will definitely be audited first. I think it is more important to keep records in advance, rather than guessing when the regulation will start or who will be audited first. What preparations should Web3 practitioners make before 2027? AKI: For Web3 practitioners and high-net-worth investors, what things should be addressed before the implementation of CARF in Hong Kong? Calix: I believe the first thing to change is one's attitude towards tax issues. As exchange KYC, anti-money laundering, and international tax information exchange systems gradually improve, crypto is entering a regulatory environment closer to traditional finance. Many investors in the past have not systematically organized their asset sources, transaction records, and tax status, which may lead to higher compliance costs in the future. For individuals holding substantial amounts of crypto assets, it is crucial to review the acquisition methods, historical transactions, fund flows, and relevant supporting documentation as early as possible, while also confirming their tax residency status in different regions. For Web3 companies, it is necessary to assess potential tax and reporting obligations based on actual business activities, company registration location, management team location, and business nature. If there are complex cross-border income, token compensation, or historical investment returns, professional tax advice can be sought in advance to explore applicable legal tax arrangements. The significance of CARF is not to require all crypto asset holders to pay a new tax, but rather to make it easier for tax authorities to obtain transaction information and determine tax obligations based on existing laws. Rather than waiting until information exchange begins to explain historical assets, it's better to establish complete asset and tax records in advance and make long-term plans while adhering to compliance.
